title: Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics and Concept of Temperature
short_intro: The Zeroth law of thermodynamics establishes thermal equilibrium as an equivalence relation between thermodynamic systems. It provides the logical foundation for the existence of temperature as a fundamental state property.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of thermal equilibrium, statement and physical significance of the Zeroth law, and the working principle of mercury-in-glass and constant-volume gas thermometers.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Transitivity property of thermal equilibrium, mathematical formulation using empirical temperature functions, thermodynamic temperature scale, and microscopic justification via the kinetic theory of gases.

prerequisites: Concept of macroscopic thermodynamic systems and boundaries
Thermal contact, diathermic and adiabatic walls
Equation of state for ideal gases

concept_notes.heading: Thermal Equilibrium and Diathermic Walls
bullets: Two systems are in thermal contact if they can exchange energy in the form of heat through a conducting boundary known as a diathermic wall.
An adiabatic wall is an insulating boundary that prevents any heat transfer between systems.
Thermal equilibrium is reached when macroscopic properties (such as pressure, volume, and electrical resistance) of systems in thermal contact cease to change with time.

concept_notes.heading: Statement of the Zeroth Law
bullets: If system A is in thermal equilibrium with system C, and system B is also in thermal equilibrium with system C, then system A and system B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
Mathematically, if T_A = T_C and T_B = T_C, then T_A = T_B.
This law forms the basis of temperature measurement, validating the use of a third system (thermometer).

concept_notes.heading: Concept of Temperature
bullets: Temperature is a scalar property that determines whether a system is in thermal equilibrium with other systems.
It is a macroscopic manifestation of the average translational kinetic energy of constituent molecules derived from the kinetic theory of gases.
Temperature equality is a necessary and sufficient condition for the absence of net heat flow between two bodies in thermal contact.

concept_notes.heading: Empirical Temperature Scales
bullets: An empirical temperature scale is constructed using a thermometric property X of a substance that varies monotonically with temperature.
Linear interpolation between two fixed reference points (ice point and steam point) defines temperature as t(X) = 100 \times \frac{X_t - X_0}{X_{100} - X_0}.
Different thermometers may yield slightly different empirical temperatures intermediate to the fixed points due to non-linear properties of thermometric substances.

derivations.title: Existence of Empirical Temperature Function
derivations.conditions: Three thermodynamic systems A, B, and C with equations of state involving pressures and volumes.
steps: Let system A have equation of state f_A(P_A, V_A) = 0, system B have f_B(P_B, V_B) = 0, and system C have f_C(P_C, V_C) = 0.
When A and C are in thermal equilibrium, their coordinates are related by a constraint equation: F_1(P_A, V_A, P_C, V_C) = 0, which can be solved to express P_C = g_1(P_A, V_A, V_C).
Similarly, when B and C are in thermal equilibrium, P_C = g_2(P_B, V_B, V_C).
Equating the two expressions for P_C eliminates V_C, yielding a relation between the coordinates of A and B: h(P_A, V_A) = k(P_B, V_B).

The Zeroth law implies that this same relation holds when A and B are in direct thermal equilibrium, meaning both functions can be equated to a universal property called empirical temperature \theta(P, V).

derivations.title: Microscopic Temperature Derivation from Kinetic Theory
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas containing N molecules enclosed in a volume V.
steps: From kinetic theory, the pressure exerted by an ideal gas is given by P = \frac{1}{3}\frac{N}{V} m \bar{v^2}.
Using the ideal gas law equation of state, PV = N k_B T, where k_B is the Boltzmann constant.
Equating the two expressions for PV gives N k_B T = \frac{1}{3} N m \bar{v^2}.
Solving for temperature yields k_B T = \frac{2}{3} \left(\frac{1}{2} m \bar{v^2}\right), where \frac{1}{2} m \bar{v^2} is the average translational kinetic energy per molecule.

formula_sheet.name: Zeroth Law Equivalence
formula_sheet.equation_html: A \sim C \text{ and } B \sim C \implies A \sim B

formula_sheet.name: Linear Thermometric Temperature Scale
formula_sheet.variables: X = thermometric property at temperature T
formula_sheet.conditions: Single fixed-point method (triple point of water)

formula_sheet.name: Ideal Gas Temperature Scale
formula_sheet.variables: PV = product of pressure and volume at low density
formula_sheet.conditions: Low pressure limit where real gas behaves ideally

formula_sheet.name: Absolute Temperature and Kinetic Energy
formula_sheet.variables: E_k = average translational kinetic energy per molecule, k_B = Boltzmann constant

formula_sheet.name: Celsius and Kelvin Conversion
formula_sheet.variables: T = absolute temperature, t = Celsius temperature

formula_sheet.name: Fahrenheit and Celsius Conversion
formula_sheet.variables: t_{^{\circ}C} = Celsius temperature, t_{^{\circ}F} = Fahrenheit temperature

formula_sheet.name: Constant Volume Gas Thermometer Relation
formula_sheet.variables: P = pressure at temperature T, P_{tr} = pressure at water triple point

formula_sheet.name: Resistance Thermometer Relation
formula_sheet.variables: R = electrical resistance at temperature T, R_{tr} = resistance at triple point

graphs_and_experiments.title: Constant-Volume Gas Thermometer Isotherms
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of pressure P versus temperature T (in Celsius) for various low densities of a gas extrapolated to absolute zero.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: All straight lines intersect the temperature axis at a single point, -273.15 \text{ } ^\circ C, which defines the absolute zero of temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in TGT/PGT to identify the universal nature of the absolute zero intercept independent of the working gas density.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Triple Point Cell of Water
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic diagram of a cylindrical glass vessel containing ice, water, and water vapor in thermal equilibrium under its own vapor pressure.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Establishes a unique, unvarying temperature reference point (273.16 K at 0.01 \text{ } ^\circ C and 611.65 Pa) used to calibrate modern thermometers.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual and factual questions regarding why the triple point is preferred over ice and steam points.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Thermometric Property vs Temperature Non-Linearity
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A non-linear curve plotting a generic thermometric property X against empirical temperature compared to a straight diagonal line.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Different thermometric materials show deviations from one another because their physical properties do not vary linearly in the exact same manner with temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Helps explain why gas thermometers are taken as standard over liquid-in-glass thermometers.

solved_numericals.question: On a new scale of temperature (called the N scale), the freezing point of water is 0^\circ N and the boiling point is 150^\circ N. What is the temperature on the Celsius scale corresponding to 60^\circ N?
solution_steps: Use the linear temperature scale conversion formula: \frac{X - X_0}{X_{100} - X_0} = \frac{C - 0}{100 - 0}.
Substitute the given values for the N scale: X = 60, X_0 = 0, X_{100} = 150.

solved_numericals.question: The resistance of a platinum resistance thermometer at the ice point (0^\circ C) is 5.00 \Omega and at the steam point (100^\circ C) is 5.23 \Omega. When the thermometer is immersed in a hot liquid, its resistance becomes 5.79 \Omega. Calculate the temperature of the liquid on this platinum scale.
solution_steps: Assume a linear relation between resistance and temperature: t = \frac{R_t - R_0}{R_{100} - R_0} \times 100.
Substitute the given values: R_0 = 5.00 \Omega, R_{100} = 5.23 \Omega, and R_t = 5.79 \Omega.

solved_numericals.question: A constant-volume gas thermometer registers a pressure of 1.50 \times 10^4 \text{ Pa} at the triple point of water (273.16 K). What pressure will it register when immersed in a chamber maintained at 350 K?
solution_steps: For a constant volume gas thermometer, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature: \frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}.
Identify knowns: P_1 = 1.50 \times 10^4 \text{ Pa}, T_1 = 273.16 \text{ K}, T_2 = 350 \text{ K}.
Rearrange to solve for P_2: P_2 = P_1 \times \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right).

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Systems in thermal equilibrium are isolated from external environmental fluctuations, which is idealized in practical setups.
Limitation: The Zeroth law establishes the existence of temperature but does not define internal energy or heat transfer magnitude, which requires the First and Second laws.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Zeroth law states that heat flows equally between three bodies in contact.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Zeroth law deals with thermal equilibrium where net heat flow is zero, not the rate or equality of heat content.
common_misconceptions.why: Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference; bodies in thermal equilibrium have no temperature difference and hence zero net heat flow.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Temperature is a measure of the total thermal energy contained in a body.
common_misconceptions.correct: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the molecules, independent of system size.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal energy (internal energy) depends on the total mass and number of particles, whereas temperature is an intensive property.

quick_revision: Zeroth law of thermodynamics introduces the concept of temperature and transitivity of thermal equilibrium: if A~C and B~C, then A~B.
Zeroth Law Equivalence: A \sim C \text{ and } B \sim C \implies A \sim B
Linear Thermometric Temperature Scale: T(X) = \frac{X - X_{triple}}{X_{steam} - X_{triple}} \times 273.16
